meta.task_prompt:
Implement GitHub issue #9 on this repo: "add redis caching in auth proxy for kanban endpoints."

There is already a shared Redis client at `internal/pkg/redis/main.go`, and it is
already used elsewhere in the codebase (see `internal/app/server.go` and
`internal/pkg/server/permissions/perm.go` for the existing usage pattern). Follow
that same pattern rather than inventing a new one.

Scope:
- Add caching for the read paths in `internal/pkg/server/routes/kanban.go`.
- Add cache invalidation on the corresponding write paths, so a write never
  leaves a stale cached read behind.
- Pick sane key naming and TTLs consistent with how the existing Redis usage in
  this repo does it.
- This repo currently has no test files. Do not feel obligated to introduce a
  whole test framework for this change, but do double check the code compiles
  and, if there's an easy way to sanity-check the caching behavior manually
  (e.g. a local run), do that.

When you are done, close with a single clear paragraph summarizing exactly what
you changed and why — that summary becomes the pull request's title and body
verbatim, so make it read like a real PR description, not an internal note.

code_review.summary: The diff adds read-through caching to four kanban GET handlers (GetLabel, getItem, exportKanban, getKanban) and one invalidation call (createKanban), all in internal/pkg/server/routes/kanban.go. Three of the four follow the existing GetLabels/getItems shape, reuse the repo's AddItemToRedis 24h TTL, and put the board id first in the key so the existing DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board) calls in createItem/updateItem/DeleteItem clear them. That part is reasonable. The getKanban change is broken, though. database.GetKanban returns a bare string (the board id), but GetItemFromRedis always unmarshals into map[string]interface{} and ignores the error. So every GET /kanban after the first gets a JSON `null`/empty object instead of the board id, and that lasts for 24h. The engine proved this with its own /tmp probe and shipped it anyway. The task's explicit requirement that 'a write never leaves a stale cached read behind' is also missed: comment writes (AddComment/UpdateComment/DeleteComment) change data embedded in the cached getItem payload and invalidate nothing. Finally, the PR description contradicts the diff. It says read caching was not implemented, but the diff implements it. That breaks the task's requirement that the closing summary describe exactly what changed.

findings.summary: getKanban caches a bare string with map-only cache helpers, so every cache hit returns JSON null/{} instead of the user's board id.
findings.failure_scenario: A user loads the kanban page and GET /kanban misses the cache, so the handler runs AddItemToRedis(userAccount+":Kanban", "<boardId>") and stores the JSON string "\"<boardId>\"". On every later request within 24h, GetItemFromRedis's Get succeeds, json.Unmarshal into map[string]interface{} fails silently, and a typed nil map comes back as a non-nil interface{}. The HIT branch then responds with c.JSON(200, <nil map>), i.e. `null` with a JSON content type, instead of c.String(200, boardId). The frontend can no longer find the user's board, so the kanban feature breaks for every user from their second visit on. The engine's own run_command at trace line 89 printed 'treated as HIT with garbage data'.
findings.suggested_fix: Don't route this value through GetItemFromRedis/AddItemToRedis. Either use redis.Rdb.Get/Set directly with a raw string and the same 1*86400*time.Second TTL, and on a hit respond with c.String(http.StatusOK, val). Or wrap it as map[string]interface{}{"board_id": res} on write and unwrap on read, keeping c.String in both branches so the response shape doesn't change.

findings.summary: The new getItem cache (and the board-keyed export cache) is never invalidated by the comment write handlers, although the Item payload embeds its comments.
findings.failure_scenario: A user opens an item (GET /kanban/item?id=X), which caches `<board>:item:X` for 24h. They then post a comment (POST /kanban/comment?item_id=X). AddComment calls kanban.AddComment and touches no cache, so reopening the item returns the cached payload without the new comment, for up to 24h. Edits and deletes behave the same way. This is exactly the 'write leaves a stale cached read behind' case that task.md forbids. The coder confirmed from kanban.proto (trace line 46/49) that Item.comments is a nested field and noted the gap as unfinished.
findings.suggested_fix: In AddComment, UpdateComment and DeleteComment, call redis.DeleteAllKeysPrefix(request.Header.Get("X-Board")), matching what createItem/updateItem/DeleteItem already do. If X-Board isn't reliably sent on comment requests, delete the specific `<board>:item:<item_id>` and `<board>:Export` keys instead. Guard against an empty board so DeleteAllKeysPrefix("") never runs.

findings.summary: The PR title and body say only create-path invalidation was done and read caching was 'not completed', but the diff adds read caching to four handlers, so the description misstates the change.
findings.failure_scenario: task.md requires the closing paragraph to 'summarize exactly what you changed', because it becomes the PR title and body word for word. A maintainer reading PR #18 is told caching isn't implemented. They'd either miss that four endpoints changed behavior, including the broken getKanban, or approve it thinking it's a harmless one-liner. Meanwhile the body never mentions the known getKanban regression that the orchestrator itself reported.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the PR title and body to list the actual edits (the four read-through caches with their key schemes and the createKanban invalidation) and the known open issues (getKanban string caching, comment invalidation), or fix those issues before opening the PR.

findings.summary: The GetLabel and getItem cache keys depend on the optional X-Board header, which the underlying lookups don't use, so a request without the header caches under `:Label:<id>` / `:item:<id>`, which no write path clears.
findings.failure_scenario: A client calls GET /kanban/item?id=X without an X-Board header. The key becomes `:item:X`. A later updateItem sends X-Board and runs DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board), which never matches `:item:X`, so header-less reads keep returning the stale item for 24h. This only matters if some client omits the header; the existing getItems handler makes the same assumption.
findings.suggested_fix: Skip caching (or return 400) when X-Board is empty, or key by resource id alone and invalidate that specific key from the write handlers.

findings.summary: The key segment casing is inconsistent with the repo's existing keys and between the new keys themselves (`:Label:`, `:Export`, `:Kanban` vs `:item:`).
findings.failure_scenario: Existing keys use `:Labels` and `:items:page:`. The new keys mix capitalised `:Label:`/`:Export`/`:Kanban` with lowercase `:item:`, which makes keys harder to grep or debug in redis-cli. This doesn't change behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one casing convention, e.g. lowercase to match `:items:`, or add small key-builder helpers.

process_review.summary: The orchestrator started well with a thorough ask survey, but it also spawned a stray 'placeholder' ask agent (trace line 3) that did nothing. The coder then re-read most of what the survey had already reported: kanban.go, redis/main.go, routes/main.go, list_files, StructToMap. It also read RPC/kanban/main.go in full, even though the survey had already listed its symbols. It respected read-before-edit: kanban.go was read at lines 34/36 before the first str_replace at line 67, so there were zero violations. It made four small, correct-looking edits. Then it spent its last three tool calls writing throwaway /tmp Go programs (lines 82, 87, 89) to probe json.Unmarshal behaviour, instead of fixing the bug it had found or running `go build ./...`. loop_control flagged repeating_itself=0.65 (line 90) and the run stopped early. The task asked for a compile check. No run_command against the repo build ever appears in the trace; the only evidence is the per-edit LSP 'no new diagnostics' lines. The write_gate judge flagged the GetLabel edit (line 69, matches_stated_intent 0.14, non-enforced), and the coder never revisited it. The orchestrator's final message accurately listed the gaps and asked the user whether to continue. Even so, a PR was opened from the partial worktree, with a body that contradicts the diff. Cost ($0.90, 45 tool calls, about 10 min wall time) is fine for a single-file change, but the run ended incomplete with a known regression.

findings.summary: The task explicitly asked to 'double check the code compiles', but no `go build`/`go vet` run against the repo appears anywhere in the trace. All three run_command calls are isolated /tmp snippets.
findings.evidence: The run_command calls at lines 82, 87 and 89 all run `cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/niltestN.go ... go run /tmp/niltestN.go`. The coder's own summary says 'Did not run go build ./... (or any build/compile command) against the actual repo'. The only compile signal is the 'no new diagnostics' text appended to each str_replace result.

At line 89 it reads 'false map[] / treated as HIT with garbage data'. No further str_replace follows, and loop_control at line 90 returns making_progress 0.13, repeating_itself 0.65.

findings.summary: Three near-identical /tmp probe programs were run where one (or reading GetItemFromRedis, already open at line 40) would have answered the question.
findings.evidence: niltest.go (line 82) checks whether a nil map returned as interface{} is nil. niltest2.go (line 87) checks unmarshalling a string into a map. niltest3.go (line 89) repeats niltest2 without the error print and adds a 'treated as HIT' println. GetItemFromRedis's `json.Unmarshal([]byte(val), &data)` with the error ignored was already visible in the line-40 read_file result.

In transcript.md, the orchestrator asks the user 'I'd like your go-ahead before I continue', and then '[worktree coder b4d9ffa3 pr] opened pull request ... /pull/18'. findings.evidence: Of the coder's tool calls from line 34 to line 89, only the str_replaces at lines 71 ('Now update `GetLabel`:') and 76 ('Now `getItem`:') have non-empty reasoning. The run_commands at lines 82, 87 and 89 have "reasoning": "".

strengths: Three of the four new read caches match the repo's existing GetLabels/getItems pattern exactly: same helpers, same 24h TTL, same X-cache: HIT header.
Keys are prefixed with the board id, so the existing DeleteAllKeysPrefix(board) calls in createItem/updateItem/DeleteItem clear them without new wiring.
createKanban invalidates the per-user getKanban key.
Read-before-edit was respected throughout, and the change stays in the one file the task named.
The engine's closing chat messages to the user were candid about the regression and the missing work.
concerns: getKanban returns null/{} instead of the board id on every cache hit, which breaks the main kanban entry point for all users after their first request.
Comment writes don't invalidate the cached item payload that embeds comments, missing the task's no-stale-reads requirement.
The PR description contradicts the diff and leaves out the known regression.
No compile or build command was ever run against the repo, even though the task asked for one.
A PR was opened from a coder run that had stopped partway, while the orchestrator was still asking the user whether to continue.
overall_assessment.narrative: The diff is mostly a mechanical extension of an existing caching pattern and would be close to mergeable. But it ships one regression the engine had already proved (getKanban's cache hit returns garbage) and misses the comment-write invalidation the task explicitly required, so it needs changes before merge. The process explains why. The coder spent its budget re-reading surveyed files and writing /tmp probes instead of fixing the bug or running `go build`. loop_control stopped it, and a PR was opened anyway with a description that contradicts the code. Fixing getKanban to cache a raw string, adding invalidation to the three comment handlers, and rewriting the PR body would make this mergeable.
